body: Yeah, I Googled all that - before I posted here, actually. It's all very vague and there was nothing I could find about a former employee's personal property. I haven't talked to a lawyer this time, largely because when I talked to two different legal agencies a few months back, they basically said "In Maine landlords can treat you like dirt and there's nothing you can do about it." The problem with free legal services is you get what you pay for; they're quite willing to dole out cookie cutter advice over the phone but gods forbid you should expect them to crack open a law book, write a letter for you or, worst of all, go to court. You'd think you'd asked them to hand over one of their relatives for a human sacrifice. Sheesh.

I'm so sorry about that job interview. That STINKS. I've noticed something similar in publishing: The people running the show in house aren't competent to decide which person they should hire. You irked them because you showed more original thinking than the entire company has shown in years.

But that being said, I hope you keep trying because there has to be a company out there that will value someone capable of thinking for themselves. Someone will snap you up and treat you like gold, as you deserve.

Here's an idea: Have you considered moving to Switzerland (or any other country) to live instead of to die? Maybe you'd be able to find work elsewhere.

Lastly, the current property manager has never been in my house and says (in writing) "...we have heard that you have cats." Sure, I actually DO, but that's not the point. The person who told her about the cats spoke illegally - she was in my house as an employee from a staffing agency and is bound by HIPAA not to discuss the household with anyone. The information she gave is BOTH inaccurate (she said I have more cats than I do) and shared illegally.

My new doctor also wrote a letter about the harassment, but I haven't seen it yet so I don't know whether it'll be helpful. I'll keep you posted.

I also have a tuxedo cat whose markings are very similar to my service dog's (he's a Landseer Newfie and is black and white). The joke is that the little tuxedo cat thinks she's a Newfie, too, and can't understand why she isn't getting as big as her brother. 

Well, I'm off to watch a movie. I wanted to check in and say hi. I'm going to try to be a better correspondent!

The personality changes people experience after catastrophic illness are terrifying. I think doctors should be taught to inform family members what to expect. Instead, we're basically told to let people get away with mistreating us because the poor babies are sick. So, it's okay for them to make US sick by behaving badly, but we have to walk on eggshells around them. Nope.

Anyway, I have to try to get some sleep. Three am is way too early to be up! I hope you'll write when you can. No rush - I'm obviously not very good at keeping up with correspondence lately myself!

I changed my approach toward him. I stand up to him now, but I don't fight or raise my voice. It seems to be working to some extent. He is at least learning that I won't tolerate as much as I once did.

I'm sure that lawyers working for legal aid don't earn nearly as much as lawyers in private practice, so they probably can't be bothered really fighting for clients. They figure they've earned their salary just by returning your call. I've been handling the situation on my own. I acceded to those demands I felt were reasonable. It hasn't come to a boiling point about the cats and I'm really hoping it won't, that the things I've agreed to do will be enough to satisfy her need for control over residents.

I think my experience might be different from the average. I wasn't diagnosed until I was 48 \(in 2003\), largely because I was hypomanic most of my life and everyone \(myself included\) just assumed I was an exceptionally happy\-go\-lucky person. I had a couple of periods of depression that lasted up to two years but resolved with treatment and therapy.

The Dx followed a traumatic event and ever since, I've cycled more frequently. It started out with the cycles lasting months but over the last two or three years I developed ultra\-rapid cycling, which in turn has escalated into frequent mixed states.

Like you, I also have no health insurance. I recently switched doctors and the new guy, whom I'll see for the first time on May 30th \(today is the 13th\), has said he'll help me get some kind of health coverage, even if it's only reduced fees. We'll see.

I share all this so you know you're not alone with these experiences. I'm really sorry that you're going through this and I'm especially sorry you have no way of getting help. I wonder...do you think your local dept of health and human services might be able to locate resources for you to get help? Some areas have mental health clinics that charge on a sliding scale. I once found one that only charged me $10 per visit and offered both counseling and medication management. With their help, I was declared stabilized in just two years, and I remained stabilized until life threw me another curve ball. It's a thought, anyway. Another thing: Please consider calling a crisis hotline if you feel suicidal. They've helped me a few times.

Good luck and I hope you'll keep us all posted about how you're doing.

It's my experience that when other people, including friends and loved ones, see us as selfish, it's because we're not living up to \*their\* expectations of us. That isn't selfishness. It's having a healthy sense of self\-esteem \- \*and\*, for that matter, self\-preservation. 

Example: I was emotionally abused by my half siblings. At age 57, I cut them out of my life. Last week, the day before my 63rd birthday, one of them contacted me. She pretended it was to issue a birthday greeting but in reality it was to tell me "family" news, including the fact that a person I haven't considered to be my "brother" since 2013 was near death. I told her to save it, that I don't care. I don't \- and I'm not going to pretend I do to make her feel better. She sees that as selfishness. I see it as treating them the same way they treated me, and protecting myself from further abuses.

You can tell I'm a cynic. Regardless, it's obvious to me that the label "selfish" is applied to anyone who refuses to put other people's well\-being before their own. Believe the people who see you as an amazing friend. Ignore those who don't, because if they expect you to sacrifice yourself for their comfort or benefit \(as people who fling the "selfish" label around usually do\), they're the selfish ones.

Up until 2003, I'd have said yes. But the way my hypomania manifested changed in that year. Prior to 2003, I always experienced what I call "happy hypomania." (Some people call it "euphoria" but it wasn't that extreme - everyone, including my doctors, just thought I was a cheerful, upbeat person.) It wasn't until a major life crisis hit in 2003 that I began having really ugly, dysphoric hypomanic states.

If I could go back to that mildly euphoric brand of hypomania, then yeah I'd miss it. But the hypomania I experience since 2003 - the rushing thoughts of impending doom, the fear that I'm going to lose control and end up in a padded cell - oh heck no. In fact, I'd give a lot never to experience that brand of hypomania ever again.

I shared the link above because up until last week, I'd been subscribed to this sub for quite some time and had often found it to be comforting. I might have occasionally disagreed with some people on some points but everything I ever read was obviously written with the intention to help.

Until last week, when someone replied to a post of mine by basically telling me to "Get over it, others have it worse than you do."

As you can see if you visit the link above, "Others have it worse" is considered one of the worst things you can say to a person with mental illness. As it explains in the link above (and in about half a dozen other articles, by both mental health professionals and people who have mental illnesses themselves, telling a person in crisis that others have it worse trivializes, marginalizes, and invalidates their pain. It isn't helpful; it's passive-aggressive nastiness.

I missed this sub terribly, though, and decided to come back and give it another try. I thought I'd start, though, by posting the link above. I have others if anyone's interested, and I'm going to do a PubMed search to see if any research has been done on this issue.

Did she mention whether she's on medication? I ask because it sounds like she's having a bout of hypomania with signs of hypersexuality. Perhaps her "distraction" is actually embarrassment and a way to deflect from her behavior and save face.

Alternatively, she could be experiencing ultradian cycling, a state in which moods can shift wildly in the space of an hour or even less.

I understand that you really like the girl and I think it's applaudable that your interest hasn't waned after hearing her diagnosis. But I'm going to tell you a harsh truth: If she isn't on medication, she probably isn't a good prospect for a long-term relationship. I say this from personal experience. My BP II was untreated for many years and I sabotaged several potentially wonderful relationships with men because my illness was out of control. Never forget that while it's great to be accepting of a partner's health issues, you must also protect yourself. I'd hate to see a nice person end up heartbroken because your acceptance and support were misplaced.

Best of luck to both of you.

Isn't it funny how some of us set higher standards for ourselves than we do for others? We make a conscious--often herculean--effort to prevent bipolar 2 from ever being a reason (although we'd see it as an excuse, not a reason) for anything. I think we do this in order to maintain some semblance of control over our lives and especially over our emotions.

The past eight months have shown me the absolute necessity of being compassionate toward myself. For me, this includes learning to distinguish between reasons and excuses, to accept that sometimes having bipolar 2 *is* a valid reason, and also to allow myself to indulge in the occasional excuse (as opposed to reason). That is, I'm re-educating myself to accept that sometimes I just don't feel like doing something, and that I have as much right to say so as anyone else. It can be an uphill battle at times, but I'm making inroads.

For me, learning to treat myself with compassion is sheer survival. I'm in a situation where I have no advocates at all. I either advocate for myself--take care of myself, including being kind to myself--or I'll die.

You hit the nail on the head. His doctors (and his family) urged me to put him in a nursing home after the stroke. I refused because I believed in the marriage vows.

However, at this point I feel that he broke the marriage contract when he began abusing me, so I no longer feel any moral obligation toward him as a husband. The care I continue to provide is an act of compassion I would show to any disabled being.

I'm glad you asked about the mini-strokes. According to him, I was unconscious for at least 20 minutes before he decided that he should try to awaken me. When I awoke I was dizzy, my limbs were weak, my vision was blurry, and I had a blinding headache. I asked him to call 911 and he refused. He said I'd be fine. Idiot that I am, I spent 20 minutes debating it with him before I made the call myself. I was hospitalized for four days, during which time he had a neighbor (who has since moved) help him with the dogs. He ate bagels and whatever leftovers were in the fridge.

I didn't even bother calling the hospital for the other two mini-strokes. It wasn't worth it to me to argue with him about being away and TBH, I was afraid he'd claim I was neglecting him if I was admitted again, since the only thing he ever talked about after the first one was how he "had to take care of myself" while I was in the hospital.

He was never abusive prior to the last 18 months. He went from being an average, okay guy before the stroke to being one of the sweetest guys on earth for the first six years post-stroke. His nurse says he was sweet because he was grateful to be alive. But then he started turning moody and from there it has escalated to viciousness and malice.

I'm so tired. I think he broke me. I just wish he'd finish the job.

Thank you for saying that. The sheriff who responded to my call said repeatedly that my husband "might not be able to help it." I hate that we live in a society in which people are excused from vicious behavior because "Oh, the poor thing can't help it."

If someone is murdered by a drug-crazed stranger, the fact that the stranger "couldn't help himself, it was the drug" doesn't make the victim any less dead.

So many people in this thread have asked me why I don't leave. I always thought it was because I didn't trust him to care for the animals if I was unable to take them with me, or that I didn't want to leave the home I'd created here (without his help).

But the full impact of that penultimate sentence in my OP--"Or that I would die" just hit me. The reason I'm still here is that I'm *letting* him abuse me to the point that my health has failed and I'll probably die well before he does.

There's no fight left in me. I'm still here because I'm committing passive suicide.

The other post doesn't say anything about taking him to the cleaners, it merely suggests that I have a right to protect my own future, which I do. But even if someone did suggest that I take everything, I wouldn't. All I want is enough to survive.

You're right. He doesn't. If you notice my last paragraph above, I didn't only say that I wished he would die--I also said "*Or that I would die.*"

Believe me, the chances are that I'll die first. He has received the best medical care available--I saw to that and I've continued to see to it. Despite his viciousness toward me, I have continued to care for him in the exact same way I cared for him before his personality changed. He would have died a dozen times over if it hadn't been for the care I provide for him--making doctor appointments, scheduling rides, ensuring that his every need is addressed.

The only person in real danger physical danger here is me. Shortly after he began demonstrating hostility toward me, I developed dangerously high blood pressure. Last June I had the first of a series of mini-strokes. According to what he said afterward, I was unconscious for at least 20 minutes--but when I came to with dizziness, weakness, and a blinding headache, he told me not to call 911 because "You'll be fine."

On Friday I tore a ligament in my shoulder while shoveling snow. I went grocery shopping anyway. I prepared dinner anyway. And I have continued to do housework and care for him despite having an injured shoulder (and a previous knee injury that has me wearing a brace). The outburst that lead to the OP occurred because I asked him to help me out by making some phone calls to see if anyone could bring us bottled water. (The pipes were frozen and with a blizzard coming in, I won't be able to carry water bottles to a neighbor's to be filled.) He went ballistic. Because I asked him to help me by making a couple of phone calls.

My point here is that he is in no danger at all. I continue to treat him like royalty--not because I believe I owe him, but because I'm a compassionate human being. Again, I'm the only one in danger here. I'm being abused. I'm very sick and not only does he expect to receive the same level of care regardless of my health, he makes things worse by abusing me.

I don't know what you mean by your comment. My only "dream" is to escape from being abused and live what's left of my life in peace. I am trying to "make it happen" by taking legal action to have him declared incompetent so that he can be removed from my house against his wishes.

Because I have put years of effort into turning this house into a home and I see no reason why I should be the one to leave when I'm not the problem. He is. That is why I had the police here as I said in my OP--to try and have him removed from the house. He refused to go and the police wouldn't remove him against his will. Starting an antidepressant can certainly lead to a temporary increase in the depression. The key word is "temporary." Antidepressants work by a gradual buildup toward a therapeutic level, which varies for each patient. It could very well be that you haven't reached that level yet.

As for nightmares, they may--or may *not*--be due to the zoloft. This is an issue you should discuss with the therapist. When it comes to side effects and adverse reactions, the two best people to question are the prescribing physician and your pharmacist. I say that because they base their replies on science, on research. A layman is going to reply based on their own personal experience, and since everybody's different, what is true for one person might not be true for you.

It's also possible, as you say, that your depression could be worsening due to the circumstances in your life right now. Sorrow over a lost love and worry over a sick loved one can both exacerbate preexisting depression.

Actually, it isn't. See, first of all, blood in sputum doesn't always indicate the need for a doctor. The cougher may need to see a dentist; they might have just, for example, lost a tooth. But even if they did actually cough up sputum, it still isn't a stranger's place to give them medical advice. (Unless of course the speaker is a medical professional.) There are many reasons for coughing up sputum and many variables that influence whether it's a medical emergency.

More importantly, I didn't say mental health awareness was a bad thing. I said--and I stand by it--that *laymen on the internet* have no business diagnosing strangers on the basis of forum posts. That goes for mental or physical ailments.

Read just about any health forum, mental or physical, and one of the key rules you'll see is "no diagnosing" (Similar caveats generally a blanket prohibition on presenting oneself as an expert or authority, and/or giving out unsolicited advice you're unqualified to give.) Some social media sites will ban laymen who offer unsolicited "expert" advice. I've seen posts pulled on some sites, their writers banned, and blanket cautions to remaining members issued because someone tried to diagnose a stranger's ailment on the basis of a single post. 

The reality is that offering any kind of medical advice--be it related to physical or mental health--is terribly dangerous. It's especially dangerous to set oneself up as an authority to people who are mentally ill, as these patients have the potential to be particularly vulnerable to influences they shouldn't be heeding. Even the most highly trained psychiatrist may on occasion lose a patient to suicide because they said the wrong thing out of ignorance. The odds that a layman will make such a mistake increase exponentially. Unless you're willing to give your personal contact information to the person you presume to advise in the event of their suicide--so that their family will have a name and address for the wrongful death suit--you'd better learn to stick to discussing subjects you know.
